actual_action: FDA did not allow the thalidomide application to become effective; Frances Kelsey continued to require scientifically reliable safety evidence despite repeated company pressure.
later_evidence: By late 1961 researchers in Germany and Australia linked thalidomide exposure in pregnancy to clusters of severe congenital abnormalities.
The drug was withdrawn from the German market in November 1961 and was never marketed in the United States under the application at issue.

The FDA chronology of 17 April 1962 records a further incomplete-application letter on 23 February 1961, followed by a separate telephone call that day. The candidate cutoff precedes that letter and excludes the subsequent call and later pregnancy-safety discussions. Its narrow evidence-limit statement does not exclude the neurological-toxicity reports already received by the reviewer.
outcomes: Thousands of severe birth defects were eventually associated with thalidomide internationally.
The US avoided the scale of exposure seen in countries where the drug had been marketed, although investigational distribution still exposed some US patients.
The episode contributed to major 1962 reforms strengthening drug safety/effectiveness and clinical-research regulation.
later_reviews_or_findings: FDA's historical accounts credit Kelsey's insistence on adequate evidence with preventing a much larger US public-health tragedy.

The case is a positive-control example of refusing an irreversible population exposure while safety evidence remained materially inadequate, rather than an argument that uncertainty always justifies prohibition.
